message.reasoning:
I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I have $20 and am on Indiana Avenue. I own three properties with one to two houses each, plus one Get Out of Jail Free card. My railroads are mortgaged. Player 1 has $247 and a red monopoly with Park Place and Boardwalk fully upgraded. Player 3 is in jail with limited cash and mortgaged properties.

Player 4 has $657 and owns light blue properties with four houses each, plus two railroads and utilities. I just paid $90 rent to Player 1 after selling one house on St. Charles Place. I can trade with Players 1, 3, and 4, but I cannot mortgage or unmortgage any properties right now.

I cannot mortgage or unmortgage anything because I lack the cash. Building is impossible with only $20. I can sell houses from States Avenue and Virginia Avenue, but St. Charles Place has just one house so it cannot be reduced further.

My pink monopoly is my main income source. Player 4's light blues at four houses are dangerous. Player 1's dark blues are heavily built and costly. My Tennessee Avenue blocks Player 4 from completing an orange monopoly. I will roll from Indiana Avenue next turn.

I am calculating the rent for each property on my next roll from Indiana Avenue. I am checking standard Monopoly rent tables to determine how much I will pay if I land on the red properties.

Indiana Avenue rent is $90 with one house. Illinois Avenue with one house costs $100. The next roll from Indiana lands on B&O Railroad, which would cost $50 if Player 4 owns both railroads. Atlantic Avenue would cost $44 under the yellow monopoly. Ventnor Avenue with one house would cost $130.

Marvin Gardens costs $120 with one house. The next roll lands on Go to Jail. Pacific Avenue and Pennsylvania Railroad are mortgaged, so they cost nothing. The most dangerous roll from Indiana is landing on Park Place with three houses, which would cost $1100.

Selling houses from States Avenue and Virginia Avenue would raise cash to $170. That covers the $130 rent on Ventnor Avenue.

Marvin Gardens costs $120, which two house sales exactly cover. Selling all five houses would raise cash to $270, but that still cannot pay the $1100 rent on Park Place. I am weighing whether to trade, since giving away Tennessee Avenue would let Player 4 complete an orange monopoly and build on it.

I will not sell Tennessee Avenue to Player 4. They already have light blue properties at four houses, so an orange monopoly would be too dangerous. I need to keep my Get Out of Jail Free card for myself.

Player 1 already owns the red monopoly and has no need for my properties. Player 3 already holds the yellow monopoly and is in jail with limited cash, so he cannot pay much. The only viable trade target is Player 4, who wants Tennessee Avenue to complete an orange monopoly. I am considering selling it to Player 4 for $90, though the buyer would inherit the mortgaged status.

Player 1 might buy Tennessee Avenue to block Player 4 from completing an orange monopoly, but he already owns dark blues and reds and may not want to spend cash. Player 3 is too weak to stop Player 4. Selling houses to cover the next roll would weaken my pink income source.

I am weighing specific trade offers to raise cash without giving up my pink monopoly. Player 4 recently paid $1100 in rent and collected $200 passing GO, so they now have $657 and are extremely rich. Player 1 remains the most dangerous opponent with fully upgraded dark blues and reds. My only realistic win condition is to survive as the last non-bankrupt player.

The bank has only three houses left. Building three more on my pink properties would cost $300, which I cannot afford with just $20. My current two-house holdings on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue are a modest threat. Reaching three houses would raise rent to roughly $450 per property, which could damage Player 4's light blue income.

The housing shortage is severe. Only three houses remain in the bank, and Player 1 has four houses on Boardwalk while Player 4 has four on each light blue. I have five houses total. If I can raise cash to build, I will claim those last three houses and deny them to the other players.

Player 1 might want to build more on the red monopoly or upgrade Boardwalk with a hotel. Selling my Get Out of Jail Free card could raise cash without giving up Tennessee Avenue or my pink properties. Player 3 is in jail with no cards and only $114, so he may be willing to pay for it.

Player 3 is safer in jail and may not want to buy a Get Out of Jail Free card. Player 4 does not need one since he is not in jail. The best trade options are selling the card for $50–100, or offering mortgaged Tennessee Avenue to Player 1 to block Player 4 from completing an orange monopoly.

Player 1 already owns the red and dark blue monopolies, so giving him mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would not complete a new set. That makes the trade less appealing than blocking Player 4. I am now weighing which opponent is actually more dangerous: Player 1 with Boardwalk at four houses and Park Place at three, or Player 4 with light blues fully upgraded.

Player 1's next roll from Free Parking will not land on my pink properties. Player 4's roll from Oriental will hit St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue.

Player 4's roll from Oriental hits my pink properties on rolls three through five, yielding $50 to $180 in rent. That is manageable with their $657 balance.

My next roll from Indiana Avenue is the real danger. I will likely land on Illinois Avenue, B&O Railroad, Atlantic Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, or Marvin Gardens. Selling houses to cover those expected costs is the immediate priority.

I mapped the exact probability and cash needs for every roll from Indiana Avenue. Ventnor Avenue is the most likely landing, costing $130, followed by Marvin Gardens at $120. The worst outcome is landing on Park Place with three houses, which would cost $1100. I cannot afford to buy North Carolina Avenue with only $20.

I will keep the Get Out of Jail Free card. I can use it to leave jail safely if sent, or stay in jail where I am safe late in the game.

I will not sell houses preemptively. Player 4 can land on my pink properties on rolls three through five, so reducing those holdings now would lower the rent I collect from them. The engine will force debt resolution only when rent is actually due, and I have already handled the current debt. Trading for cash instead would let me avoid selling houses on moderate rent hits while preserving my pink income.

I need roughly $130 to survive the next roll without selling houses. Selling the Get Out of Jail Free card for $50–100 would not cover Ventnor Avenue’s $130 rent, and it would sacrifice my ability to leave jail freely. Mortgaged Pennsylvania Railroad is another option, but Player 4 already owns two railroads and could use a third to collect $100 in rent.

Player 4 could pay $50–80 for mortgaged Pennsylvania Railroad, but that is too little. Player 1 might pay more for Tennessee Avenue, yet an orange monopoly would be lethal. Player 4 has only $657 and would need roughly $484 in unmortgage costs plus house upgrades to build on those properties.

Player 1 could pay up to $247 for Tennessee Avenue, but he needs that cash to survive light blue rent and build on his own monopolies. He cannot reach my pink properties from Free Parking, so the trade would not help him land there immediately.

Player 1 might only pay $50–100 for mortgaged Tennessee Avenue as a blocker, and Player 3 is too weak to offer a good price. The safest path is to end the turn with $20 cash, keep my two-house pink rent intact, and let the engine resolve any debt on my next roll. That preserves the $150–$180 I would collect from Player 4 if they land on my pinks.

Player 4’s expected rent from my pinks is only about $35. I will propose a trade now, since Player 3 is in jail and the next active players are Player 4 and then Player 1.

I am unsure whether a trade proposal resolves immediately or waits for the target player to respond. If Player 4 accepts a trade now, they could unmortgage Tennessee Avenue and upgrade it before I benefit. That would strengthen them too quickly.

I will end the turn. Building, mortgaging, and trading are all impossible or harmful right now. Player 3 is in jail and unlikely to pay well for the Get Out of Jail Free card. Selling houses now would only reduce the rent I collect from Player 4. Trading Tennessee Avenue to Player 4 would be strategically dangerous, and offering it to others for a few dollars is too uncertain.

I cannot trade houses, only properties, cash, or Get Out of Jail Free cards. Player 1 has no urgent need for my card. Player 4 already owns mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue, so offering them the Pennsylvania Railroad would be pointless.

A $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would leave Player 4 with only $257. Unmortgaging all four orange properties costs roughly $484, so they cannot build on the set immediately. This makes the trade a viable way to raise cash while still blocking an orange monopoly.

Player 4 could sell all four houses on the light blue properties to raise roughly $600. That would cover the remaining $227 needed to unmortgage the orange set and build there immediately. Selling those houses would strip his main weapon, and he may not want to give away his scarce housing stock.

A $350–$450 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would still leave Player 4 short of the $484 needed to unmortgage the entire orange set, so an orange monopoly would not form immediately. That price could raise enough cash to survive the next roll and perhaps build on my own properties. I am now second-guessing whether to sell it at all, since stripping Player 4 of cash would also deepen his Boardwalk rent hole.

Player 4 cannot pay Boardwalk rent without selling houses. Even after a $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue, he would still lack the $1700 needed to cover that debt. He was already bankrupt-bound before this trade. The trade would not improve his ability to pay Boardwalk.

Player 4 cannot pay Boardwalk rent without selling houses. Selling all twelve light blue houses would raise only about $600, leaving a gap of roughly $857 against the $1700 rent. That is more than double the $1100 needed for Pennsylvania Avenue. Extracting $400 from them now would make that shortfall fatal.

Player 4 would likely reject a $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue, since that would leave them unable to survive dark blue rent and unable to unmortgage the orange set. A lower offer around $200–$250 might be acceptable instead. I am now weighing whether any reasonable trade exists, or if proposing one would only signal desperation.

A $250 offer for mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would leave Player 4 with roughly $407. That is still too little to survive Pennsylvania Avenue rent, since he would need about $1100 and only has about $1207 after selling houses and mortgaging railroads. The extraction is not large enough to make that rent fatal.

Player 4’s total liquidation is roughly $1617, which covers Pennsylvania Avenue but not Boardwalk. To make Pennsylvania Avenue fatal, his cash after extraction must fall below about $140.

Player 4 would reject a $517 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue because it would bankrupt them on Pennsylvania Avenue. A lower offer around $150–250 would still let them build an orange monopoly later, so that trade is unwise. I will instead propose mortgaged Tennessee Avenue to Player 1 for $100–150, since he has $247 and might accept the cash to block Player 4’s orange path.
